# Engine noise diagnosis

> Items marked **[Partial]** are only partly confirmed by the source and need more work. They stay in the review queue and are firmed up, corrected or removed as more sources come in.

## Summary

[Partial] Listen for a constant clatter that is loud during cold starts but fades after about 5 seconds of running time. [t772]

[Partial] Inspect the fan clutch and check for damage on the fan mount bearings caused by it. [t317]

[Partial] Spray carburetor cleaner or starter fluid around the #1 intake runner while cold. [t327]

Listen for a high-pitched whine and verify it disappears when laying off the accelerator. [t359]

Turn on and off the A/C while idling in gear to isolate a clicking sound from the compressor clutch. [t514]

Start the engine, then drive for several miles to hear if it knocks. [t773]

Locate the hose running from the transmission and inspect its connection method. [t790]

## Procedure

> **[Partial]** Needs more work: the verifier could confirm only part of this procedure (the steps marked [Partial], or whether the list is complete). Steps or precautions may be wrong or missing; read the source thread before relying on it. Later runs fill it in as more sources are found.

1. Listen for a constant clatter coming from the engine.
2. Note if the sound is loud during cold starts but fades after about 5 seconds of running time.
3. Check if a faint knock persists, especially under hard acceleration.
4. [Partial] Observe if the noise becomes louder and lasts longer when driving in really cold weather without warming up first.

_Procedure reported by [t772]._

<details><summary>Alternate procedure [t327] [Partial]</summary>

1. [Partial] Spray carburetor cleaner or starter fluid around the #1 intake runner while cold.
2. Watch for a smoothing out of idle speed to confirm vacuum leaks.

</details>

<details><summary>Alternate procedure [t359] [Partial]</summary>

1. Listen for a high-pitched whine coming from the front left when depressing the accelerator at slower speeds.
2. [Partial] Verify that the noise disappears completely when laying off the accelerator pedal.

</details>

<details><summary>Alternate procedure [t514] [Partial]</summary>

1. [Partial] Turn the A/C on and off to isolate a clicking sound from the compressor clutch.
2. [Partial] Listen closely near the engine bay while idling in gear to identify if the rattle coincides with the AC engagement.

</details>

<details><summary>Alternate procedure [t773] [Partial]</summary>

1. Start the engine and listen for a loud knocking sound.
2. [Partial] Drive for several miles to allow the oil to circulate fully through the motor.

</details>

<details><summary>Alternate procedure [t790] [Partial]</summary>

1. Locate the hose running from the transmission up toward the air box area.
2. Inspect if the hose connects to a specific port or simply clips onto the side of the air box.

</details>

## Tips & gotchas

- [Partial] Note that 2nd Gen water pumps are driven by the timing belt or chain, so they do not need replacement unless there is an issue. [t317]
- Understand that the fan runs on a separate idler bearing bolted to the front of the engine. [t317]
- Look specifically at the mating surface between the lower intake plenum and the head. [t327]
- [Partial] Use a screwdriver as a stethoscope to pinpoint internal noise sources. [t514]
- Check for loose engine mounts that may amplify vibration at stop lights. [t514]

## Common mistakes

- [Partial] Assuming the AC compressor bearings are bad without checking them first, leading to unnecessary part swaps. [t514]
